activities.anchor: a fact that surprises most people
activities.caption: call the census — where the neurons live
activities.name: batCensusEstimate

config.prompt: Of the brain's roughly 86 billion neurons, how many crowd the small, densely packed cerebellum at the back?
config.why: About 70 billion — the cerebellum holds the large majority, while the famous cortical sheet holds about 16 billion.
config.context: The cortex is the wrinkle everyone pictures; the counting surprise lives at the back of the head.

config.why: Lips and fingers need fine discrimination and fine control; backs do not. The drawing's distortions are the data, not an error — and a violinist's finger territory expands with use.

activities.anchor: you sleep through a ticking clock but wake at your name
activities.caption: true or false — the deep structures
activities.name: batDeepJudge

statements.s: Nearly all sensory traffic bound for cortex stops at the thalamus for gating.
statements.why: That gating is why a ticking clock fades but your name cuts through — and cortico-thalamic loops help maintain consciousness itself.

statements.s: Basal ganglia degeneration produces Parkinson's (too little movement) and Huntington's (too much).
statements.why: The gating-and-selection system between cortex and movement, read out in both directions of failure.

statements.s: Patient S.M., with bilateral amygdala damage, could recognise fear in faces but not feel it.
statements.why: The reverse: she could not recognise fear in faces and was effectively fearless, walking through situations most people find terrifying.

statements.s: The cerebellum holds only a small fraction of the brain's neurons.
statements.why: Roughly 69 billion — mostly tiny granule cells — make up the majority of the brain's total neuron count.

activities.anchor: Sperry and Gazzaniga showed that the two hemispheres
activities.caption: scrub the dates that drew the map
activities.name: batMapTimeline

events.title: Broca's patient 'Tan'
events.text: Left-frontal damage leaves speech almost gone but understanding intact — language anchored in the left hemisphere.

events.title: Wernicke's opposite case
events.text: Fluent but meaningless speech with failed comprehension — the map's second anchor, within a decade of the first.

events.title: Brodmann's atlas
events.text: Dozens of areas drawn purely from how cells stack; area 17 is still primary visual cortex, area 4 still primary motor.

events.title: H.M.'s resection
events.text: Both hippocampi removed to treat epilepsy — memory revealed as multiple systems.

events.title: Sperry's Nobel Prize
events.text: Split-brain work shows the hemispheres can work independently — specialisation is real, the two-personalities myth is not.

activities.anchor: not how evolution built the organ
activities.caption: find the faulty line — a pop-psychology article
activities.name: batTriuneSpot

config.prompt: An article about the brain contains one faulty line — click it:
lines: Textbook locations are averages — language areas vary by centimetres between people.
White matter occupies similar volume to cortex and carries the long-range traffic.
The brain evolved in three tidy layers: reptilian brain, limbic system, neocortex.
The same cortical patch damaged in different patients can yield different deficits when the connections differ.
config.correction: The triune layering is retired: structures overlapped, co-opted and retooled across lineages — modern comparative work rejects the layer metaphor.
config.why: The unit of function is increasingly the circuit, and plasticity is the map's fourth dimension — a scaffold whose rooms are re-carpeted constantly.
